contentFields.title: Content
contentFields.text: The role of communication in our daily lives can hardly be overestimated: it influences how we see the world around us, our relationships, our behaviour and our identity. In this course, we explore what communication is and how it comes about. We examine the role of verbal and non-verbal communication, look at communication in both an everyday and an organisational context, and explore the impact of technology on communication. In a series of lectures, we discuss various theories and the links between them, and become familiar with research in the field of CIS. We lay a strong theoretical foundation for the rest of the IBC BA programme, paying specific attention to the three specialisation profiles: People and Digital Communication, International Business Communication, and Communication with Social Impact.

contentFields.title: Aims
contentFields.text: By the end of the course, you can: describe how meaning, identity, and relationships are formed through communication describe the relationship between culture and communication explain how context and medium influence the goals and form of communication distinguish different approaches to research in the field of CIS

contentFields.title: Content
contentFields.text: This course addresses language use in the context of mediated communication. It offers an overview of some of the basic concepts and theoretical approaches in the study of language use in media. Attention will be paid to the relationship between language use and (mass) media also with consideration of production and reception aspects. Lectures will cover introduction to topics such as discourse and mediation, genre and styles, media storytelling, censorship and resistance. During the seminars, initial analysis of language use in context will be practiced in different forms of mediated communication (on real-world examples).

contentFields.title: Aims
contentFields.text: Upon successful completion of this course you can : explain central concepts and theoretical approaches in the study of language use in media; distinguish the significance of specific examples of language use in media; apply central concepts from language use in mediated communication to real-world examples; make initial analyses of language use in (mass) mediated communication.

contentFields.title: Test information
contentFields.text: The course will be graded based on an individual portfolio consisting of different assignments (pass/fail), and a final exam (digital testing via ANS), about the lectures and the course literature (minimal passing grade: 5.5).

contentFields.title: Content
contentFields.text: This course introduces students to the fundamental concepts and key phenomena of digital communication. Increasingly, communication in both private and public life takes place through digital channels. People not only interact with each other through digital means, but they also interact with computers (e.g., robots, chatbots). The central question in this course is how people communicate in digital environments. Rather than focusing on the technical workings of digital media, this course emphasizes the human side of communication—how people adapt their language and interactional strategies in the context of the affordances and constraints of digital platforms and their implications and effects. This question is approached from multiple theoretical and methodological perspectives to develop a well-rounded understanding of the forms, practices, and processes of digital communication. Taking into account that technology is constantly in flux, students will examine how the characteristics of various digital media relate to and influence the ways in which people use language in the digital world. By combining academic insight with real-world examples, the course also helps students develop analytical and critical skills that are highly relevant for careers in communication, where the ability to understand and navigate digital interaction is essential.

contentFields.title: Aims
contentFields.text: At the end of the course, students can: Explain and illustrate key concepts and terminology related to digital communication using relevant examples. Apply multiple methodological approaches and concepts to study digital communication in various contexts. Identify and explain similarities and differences of language use across different digital media platforms. Analyze the relationship between media characteristics and interactional patterns in digital communication. Examine and reflect on the interactional and contextual implications of how people use language in digital environments. Assess insights from the course for relevance within a chosen context, creatively apply these insights by translating them into a digital product, and clearly present this product to an audience of peers.

contentFields.title: Content
contentFields.text: Of all forms of communication, oral interaction is the most fundamental and rich one. This course lays the foundation for studying oral social interaction. Students are introduced to analyzing interaction using the approach of conversational analysis. Concepts covered in the first period include adjacency pairs, sequential organization, turn-taking, repair and membership categorization. These concepts are explained using concrete examples, i.e., fragments from conversations. Students also learn to transcribe a conversation excerpt themselves according to interaction analysis conventions. In groups, students select a conversation excerpt and analyze it according to the interaction analysis method, including some embedding in scientific literature. Throughout the course, students discover how the dynamics of interaction work, how much the details matter, and how interesting it is to study what people do among each other throughout the day: social interaction. In the context of international business communication, understanding how social interaction works is crucial. Students become aware of minute interactional features that impact goals, identities and relationships in professional settings across cultures.

contentFields.title: Aims
contentFields.text: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: 1. handle and apply the main concepts and their meanings from the field of interaction analysis; 2. select and transcribe a conversational excerpt according to current conventions; 3. analyze conversation excerpts for interactional aspects such as turn-taking, sequential organization and repair; 4. link a data-driven analysis to previous interaction research in an oral presentation.

contentFields.title: Content
contentFields.text: This course introduces students to the basic concepts and theories of corporate communication. The first part of the course discusses the nature of and historical developments in corporate communication, as well as the rise of social media for business. Most theories on corporate communication are based on insights into stakeholder management and the importance of a sound corporate reputation for the well-being of the organisation, which are the central concepts that are discussed in the second part of the course. The third part of the course deals with communication in practice: how is the strategy developed and implemented? How do organisations keep track of the extent to which goals are reached? The fourth part of the course focuses on some specialist areas in the field of corporate communication, such as building and maintaining relations with journalists and media, employee communication, issues management, and crisis communication. The last part of the course discusses leadership, change communication, and the growing importance of corporate social responsibility.

contentFields.title: Aims
contentFields.text: At the end of this course, a student can: Identify the most important elements of corporate communication and describe interrelationships between these elements; Distinguish the corporate communication goals of organisations and recognise the strategies organisations use to attain these goals; Understand and apply the most important insights of different specialist areas of corporate communication; Analyse actual cases of corporate communication and give informed evaluations of the success of this communication.

contentFields.title: Content
contentFields.text: The focus of this course is twofold. Firstly, it aims to introduce students to the foundations and principles of doing research. In the process, students will reflect on different research methodologies and approaches to data collection commonly used in communication research. Secondly, the course focuses on academic skills required to critically process research literature as well as academic skills required to write about research. Skills include searching for and selecting relevant sources, adopting a critical attitude towards sources, selecting and effectively integrating information from sources into own writing, creating a clear and coherent text, and using an academic writing style. Students will learn how to appropriately cite and reference sources, in accordance with the academic conventions. Finally, students will practice critical reflection on both their own and others’ academic texts.

contentFields.title: Aims
contentFields.text: This course provides an important foundation for student success in the overall BA programme, as it focuses on essential skills for studying at a university and functioning in an academic context. Such skills relate to reflecting on suitable approaches to research in Communication and Information Studies, critical reading and reasoning, effective academic writing, and constructive collaboration. The course aims to achieve the following learning objectives: Research orientation: students can identify and explain different research questions and strategies, research methodologies (e.g. qualitative and quantitative), and data types; Academic reading: students can search for, select, critically read, summarize and assess academic literature starting from a set research topic; Academic topic choice: students can determine a specific research focus on a set research topic and articulate its relevance for theory and practice, based on relevant academic sources; Academic writing: students can individually write a concise Introduction section to a research proposal (including a theoretical framework) leading to a relevant research question; Academic writing: students can individually write clear, coherent, and logically structured texts, using an academic writing style, in accordance with the academic conventions (e.g., APA referencing); Academic (peer) reviewing: students can assess their own and others’ academic writing and provide constructive feedback.

contentFields.title: Content
contentFields.text: This course offers students an introduction to intercultural communication and the factors that shape and influence it. Due to globalization, migration and international work mobility, intercultural contact between people from different cultures -and different language backgrounds- has become more common in recent decades. Societies have become increasingly multicultural. Intercultural communication is a part of life for most people, in both everyday and work contexts. For business professionals who work in an international setting, or for students studying abroad, it is important to have insight into the ways in which culture can play a role in intercultural contact situations, in terms of behaviour in general and interpersonal communication in particular. This course considers the concept of culture, and how culture influences our thinking, acting and being. It examines the influence of culture on verbal and non-verbal communication, the relationship between culture, identity and communication, and how cultural value orientations influence our worldview and the way we behave towards others. The course also considers topics such as acculturation in immigrants and expats, culture shock, and the development of intercultural (communication) competence.

contentFields.title: Aims
contentFields.text: At the end of the course, students will: Be able to identify and describe fundamental theoretical concepts and principles that are relevant to understanding communication between people from different cultural and social backgrounds; Have insight into the concept of culture, cultural differences and how culture can influence verbal and non-verbal behaviour; Have insight into contributors to - and issues in - intercultural communication, and be able to reflect critically on these; Have insight into acculturation/cultural adaptation, culture shock, and the development of intercultural communication competence, and be able to identify and critically reflect on factors that play a role in these processes.

contentFields.title: Content
contentFields.text: In many communicative contexts, the sender wants to persuade the receiver of something. Consider, for example, an advertisement where a global tech company is promoting a new software product in multiple markets, the World Health Organization that uses localised campaigns to persuade people of the importance of a healthy lifestyle, or a charity that uses a fundraising letter to convince people of the necessity of a donation to countries struggling with poverty. These are all examples of persuasive communication: communication aimed at influencing people's beliefs, attitudes, and behavior. What determines whether this communication is successful? What characteristics of the message play a role in this? And what characteristics of the sender and the receiver are important here? How is persuasive communication processed by receivers? And how do you measure the persuasiveness of a message? In this course, we will seek the answers to these crucial questions.

contentFields.title: Aims
contentFields.text: At the end of the course students: 1. have knowledge of the main theories in the field of persuasive communication 2. are able to recognize and name the central concepts from these theories 3. know which textual, linguistic, and visual elements play a role in the persuasion process 4. are able to analyze and critically evaluate practical examples of persuasive communication 5. can develop a persuasive message of which the design choices are informed by theoretical knowledge about the processing and effects of persuasive communication.

contentFields.title: Content
contentFields.text: When we communicate, we can have different goals: to inform someone, to persuade them, to explain something, to make someone laugh, etc. At the basis of all these goals lies the premise that our audience understands what we are saying. But what does it actually mean to understand a message, for instance a text or an utterance? And what factors influence whether, or how well we understand someone? This course examines how people construct meaning from communication, focusing mainly on the discourse level (i.e., beyond the sentence level). Building on the concept of situation model construction, we examine how textual and cognitive features affect discourse comprehension. In other words: we investigate how people understand a given message depending on the characteristics of a text or the way their brain works. We will cover topics such as coherence and cohesion, ambiguity, predictive processing, information structure, background knowledge, the role of context in interpretation, and multiple document comprehension. Knowing how humans make sense of communicative messages is fundamental to knowing how to strategically adapt a message to achieve a certain goal. In the second part of the course, you will put theory into practice. In small groups, you will work on creating an expository talk on a complex topic, putting careful thought into the intended audience, as well as the structure and textual features of the discourse. All considerations will be documented in an annotated version of the talk.

contentFields.title: Aims
contentFields.text: At the end of this course, you can: describe how people construct situation models on the basis of communicative input explain how features of the discourse and of the reader/listener influence comprehension analyse the coherence, cohesion, and information structure of a discourse create an explanatory text that is optimized for understanding by a particular audience, and motivate your text design choices orally present an explanation of a complex topic

contentFields.title: Content
contentFields.text: Information permeates every facet of our modern society, offering both incredible opportunities and notable risks. With the advent of AI, social media and big data, we are faced with challenges ranging from fake news to cybercrime. How can we navigate and thrive in this new and constantly changing environment? This course will equip you with the knowledge about the complexities of using AI, the World Wide Web, and social media for information searching, content creation, and dissemination. You will learn to use best practices, recognize opportunities, and understand the potential risks associated with these technologies. Human information processing and communication are also subject to numerous limitations and risks, rooted in cognitive biases and bottlenecks shaped by our biological and cultural evolution. This course will help you recognize the boundaries of human cognition and be aware of the influence of your own cultural background—an essential foundation for becoming an expert in communication and information. Additionally, the course encourages you to reflect on your own information behaviour. Do you tend to choose the path of least effort? Do you protect your mental health? Do you think about your digital footprint? This course aims to prepare you to make informed, responsible decisions in the complex world of data, information and knowledge.

contentFields.title: Aims
contentFields.text: At the end of the course, students will be able to: Describe how people create, process and communicate data, information and knowledge, and apply this knowledge for tasks in your academic and personal life. Explain how computers process data and information and how those are shared on the Internet. Appraise the opportunities and risks of generative AI tools and digital technologies in general for our society. Use the knowledge from learning goals 1,2 and 3 to critically evaluate and manage your information behaviour, including your digital footprint. Investigate existing literature on a topic of the course and represent your findings in the form of a visually effective presentation, created with the help of digital tools.

contentFields.title: Content
contentFields.text: Brands and organisations employ strategic marketing communication with the goal to positively impact the perception and behaviour of consumers and stakeholders. In this course, the student will become acquainted with the field of marketing communication, its important elements, the basic principles of marketing communication, and its persuasive goals and effects. Students will gain insights into various manifestations (or channels) of marketing communication (such as advertising, public relations, sponsorship, webcare) as well as the brand, message and media strategies that marketing communications can adopt. Students will study relevant theories and models on how marketing communication affects consumers and gain an understanding of how to evaluate the effectiveness and ethics of marketing communication campaigns. Additionally, the course aims at stimulating students’ creativity which is so indispensable in developing marketing campaigns. As such, students will use the acquired knowledge to design a marketing communication plan for a new brand, product or service in a group assignment.

contentFields.title: Aims
contentFields.text: At the end of the course, students can: Recognize and explain the role of communication in different marketing processes Name, explain, identify, and relate the principal forms and strategies in marketing communication Name and explain relevant theories, models, and research findings about the impact of marketing communication on consumer cognition, attitudes and behaviour Apply their knowledge about the topics above to design and substantiate a marketing communication plan Apply their knowledge about the topics above to analyse and critically reflect on marketing communication activities

contentFields.title: Content
contentFields.text: Research is at the center of every scientific discipline. This course acts as a first introduction to carrying out research in general and focuses specifically on survey research. We will discuss the basics of the research process, focusing on both qualitative and quantitative approaches, and paying particular attention to the function of statistics in empirical research. Topics related to descriptive statistics will be introduced (e.g., variables, measures of central tendency and dispersion, frequency distributions, normal distributions, confidence intervals, correlation and reliability coefficients). In addition, students will learn what to take into account when setting up and carrying out survey research. They will get the chance to put this knowledge into practice by carrying out their own research project (in groups) and describing and visualizing the data that they collect. Students will also learn how to report the results of (survey) research.

contentFields.title: Aims
contentFields.text: The goal of this course is to develop students' basic understanding and skills related to the research process and descriptive statistics, with a particular focus on survey research. By the conclusion of this course, students will be able to: understand the basics of the research process; understand the basics of descriptive statistics; understand the important aspects of conducting survey research; describe, visualize and interpret data (from survey research); carry out a survey research project in groups (with support from the instructor) and to write a research report about the results

contentFields.title: Content
contentFields.text: Content Working on your personal and professional development (PPD) How to make the transition to university? Which skills would you like to develop further? During coaching sessions, individually or with a group of peers, you will ponder questions like these. We will challenge you to think about who you want to be as a person and an academic. Furthermore, you will set your own goals, devise strategies and act to achieve your goals. By consciously working on your PPD (personal and professional development) you will boost your self-confidence, self-reliance and resilience. This will help you grow into a conscientious, committed, critical and self-aware academic who is set up for lifelong learning and feels ready to play their part in society. In the course manual and on Brightspace you will find additional information about coaching sessions, groups, schedule and programme.

contentFields.title: Aims
contentFields.text: Aims At the end of the course, the student is able to reflect on their personal and professional development and shape this development by identifying and substantiating their own needs and insights and by making informed choices. by engaging in activities to the benefit of their own development in the program (and for the benefit of their future career)

contentFields.title: Test information
contentFields.text: Test information During your whole bachelor’s you will work on your personal and professional development (PPD) and you will record this development in a portfolio (Portflow). You will not be graded at the end of the Mentoring program, but instead the end result is a ‘pass’ or ‘no pass’. Successfully ending your mentoring program is your first milestone in the PPD learning trajectory. The time you spend on PPD and building up your portfolio, including the time you invest during this mentoring program, will be rewarded in a course in the last/third year of your bachelor’s.

contentFields.title: Content
contentFields.text: In order to have you begin your studies successfully, you are required to take a test of academic language proficiency in your first year. If you are enrolled in an English-taught bachelor’s programme or an English-taught specialisation of a bachelor’s programme, you are to complete an academic diagnostic assessment of English: the RADAr (Radboud Academic Diagnostic Assessment) English. The objective of this test is to provide you with more information about your English language skills in an academic context. Passing this test means you have mastered the rules of spelling, grammar and punctuation governing the English language and that you are sufficiently skilled in the areas of academic vocabulary, reading, logic and argumentation. In preparation for the RADAr, you can attend an introductory lecture. Subsequently, you can practice your language skills with a digital toolbox on Brightspace. In the course of period 1, you will take the RADAr and receive an individual score report. Since a good command of academic English is essential for successfully completing your bachelor’s degree, all students have the opportunity to attend free workshops and receive writing assistance at the Radboud Writing Lab. Should you score below the norm, we strongly recommend you to register for these workshops at the Radboud Writing Lab. Were you not able to sit the exam on the first test date, but you would like to attend the workshops? Or have you passed the RADAr, but would you still like to improve yourself in certain areas? You are more than welcome to join the workshops. Participation in the introductory lecture or workshop is not compulsory (yet strongly recommended); participation in the RADAr is. For more detailed information about, for example, the time and location of the lecture and the test, please check the study guide on Brightspace.

contentFields.title: Aims
contentFields.text: After completing the course, you can apply the rules of spelling, grammar and punctuation governing the English language and will be sufficiently familiar with academic vocabulary, reading, logic and argumentation in an academic context.

contentFields.title: Content
contentFields.text: Every day, we observe and engage in different forms of discourse: Think about dinner table conversations, the news articles you check on your phone, discussions during work meetings, or a letter written to the faculty board about a certain problem experienced by students and employees on campus. In all of these cases, language is not used in a vacuum; rather, it is produced and used in a context made of communicative, cultural, social, and political factors. Similarly, these texts can represent certain perspectives and ‘ideologies’. Looking at these forms of social life and discourse from a scientific perspective, several questions arise: What happens in these situations? How do people use language, and why do they use language in a certain way? What is the function of a certain form of language use? What are the reasons behind the production of a certain type of text, and what is the potential impact of that? How can we analyze these phenomena qualitatively within their social context? In this course, you will learn to conduct systematic analysis of text and talk, following two different but related qualitative approaches, namely discourse analysis and interaction analysis. The first part (discourse analysis, period 1) will focus on fundamental concepts in the field of discourse analysis and the basics of a discourse analytical approach, qualitative analysis of text (verbal and/or visual) based on appropriate methods, and the function of textual features within the broader context of production and consumption. The second part (interaction analysis, period 2) will introduce various social scientific approaches to the study of social communication, including their theoretical underpinnings and practical applications in the form of ethnographic (non-fiction) writing, ethnomethodological observation, and in situ data collection. For each part, you will do an analysis based on actual data where you will also learn about problem definition, data collection, development of model of analysis, writing research report and/or accountability check in qualitative analysis of text and talk. The course will have a format of very short lectures and/or self-study of the theoretical material before each session and actual analysis and discussion of data during the seminars.

contentFields.title: Aims
contentFields.text: Upon successful completion of this course, the student will be able to: Explain the essence of interaction analysis and discourse analysis based on relevant theoretical concepts; Develop a (critical) perspective for systematic qualitative analysis of data; Analyze the communicative function of verbal (and visual) features within the broader context (social, political, cultural) in which the text is produced and used, with a focus on critical discourse analysis, cultural discourse analysis and framing analysis; Analyze social communication and interaction following appropriate qualitative methods, particularly ethnomethodology, ethnography and fieldwork-based methods.

contentFields.title: Content
contentFields.text: A large part of the research within IBC is experimental in nature. In this course, you will learn which factors are important when designing an experimental study. Topics covered include experimental research design, ethical guidelines for research with human participants, and validity and reliability. In addition, you will learn about statistical analyses that are typically used in experimental research. You will put this knowledge directly into practice by designing your own experimental study (conducted in groups) and by analysing and interpreting the data derived from it. Attention is also given to the reporting of experimental research (and its results). This course thereby builds on the knowledge and skills previously acquired in Data Description and Visualisation from the first year of the Bachelor's programme.

contentFields.title: Aims
contentFields.text: The aim of the course is to acquire knowledge and skills that are crucial for designing and conducting experimental research. Upon completion of the course, the student has: knowledge of aspects that are important when designing an experiment and is able to apply this knowledge in their own research (exam); knowledge of statistical analyses that are commonly used in experimental research and can interpret the output of these analyses (exam); the skills to appropriately analyse data obtained from experimental research (assignment); the skills to design and conduct experimental research in a group setting and to report on this (assignment).

contentFields.title: Content
contentFields.text: International businesses operate globally, involving stakeholders from diverse cultural and linguistic backgrounds ­­­— whether investors, employees, or customers. This international reality has made language — as a vehicle to discuss, inform, or persuade — an increasingly prominent subject of academic research in the field of international business over the last decades. Language shapes international business across virtually all domains, from HR and advertising, to strategy and negotiation. This course introduces students to the multifaceted role that language plays in international business by taking two perspectives: a theoretical perspective, grounded in current academic research, and an applied perspective, in which theoretical insights are tested against a real-life business case. The course is structured around four essential themes: employees’ identity, team work, processes of power, and language proficiency. For each theme, students first engage with the relevant academic literature before applying their understanding to a concrete business context.

contentFields.title: Aims
contentFields.text: By the end of the course, students can: Explain the theoretical frameworks that describe the role of language areas of identity, team work, and power in international business Analyse how language proficiency affects employees in international business contexts Apply their theoretical knowledge to critically examine a real-life business case, identifying how language dynamics show up in a real-life business case Reflect on the relationship between theory and practice by evaluating how well academics theories are able to account for real-world business situations

contentFields.title: Content
contentFields.text: Philosophy of Communication is a philosophy course geared specifically at students in the BA IBC. It engages philosophical theories and themes of relevance to students studying communication. Some of the themes to be addressed are: (1) The relationship between language, persuasion, and knowledge; (2) Theories of ethics as applicable to concrete case studies in the field of communication; (3) Language and politics. Additionally, this course seeks to engage prevailing existential and social themes of relevance to student’s lives as citizens of this world. Finally, by being trained in philosophical methodologies, this course offers valuable philosophical skills that are transferable to other domains, such as critical thinking, close reading, and argumentation skills.

contentFields.title: Aims
contentFields.text: At the end of the course the student will be able to: Apply and explain important philosophical concepts that are relevant to the study of communication. Read and critically evaluate philosophical texts on a basic level. Provide an ethical analysis of case studies of relevance within the field of communication.

contentFields.title: Content
contentFields.text: Is "geweldig leuk" more fun than "great fun"/"très amusant"/"muy divertido"/"ein großer Spaß"? : Corpus research into the formulation of language intensity in WOM in different languages There are a lot of review sites on the Internet: Word-of-mouth recommendations (or negative reviews) by individual users of products or services (books, films, hotels, household appliances, telecom products, etc.). These sites often use a star rating system: a user awards 0 to 5 stars as their rating and writes an accompanying review. In this course, we will research whether and how recommendations in one language/culture can be compared to recommendations in another language/culture. We will also research whether negative statements have the same effect as positive statements. Perhaps the expression of an intense review in one language is more diverse and explicit than in another. 1. Orientation to the course In this course, the student will deepen their knowledge of intercultural and cross-cultural research, from corpus research to the effects of stylistic instruments to emphasise the message. After an introduction to the fundamental principles of intercultural research, the course will work towards developing a research question on the basis of secondary literature in the area of word-of-mouth communication, communication styles, and the effects of a foreign language on non-nativeness and polarity. In the seminars of this course (period 2) you will develop your own research project and report on this in your target language (English or Spanish). 2. The role of the course in the curriculum You are in the bachelor’s phase of your studies and this course builds on the first-year courses Intercultural Communication, Corporate Communication, Communication and Persuasion, and Data Description and Visualisation. This course primarily lays a foundation in the principles of a cross-linguistic and cross-cultural corpus analysis. Furthermore, you will improve your analytical and critical skills concerning the development of an analysis model and the implementation of this analysis model in quantitative evidence-driven corpus research. Finally, you will also improve your skills in your foreign language (English or Spanish), especially your written skills in academic reporting. These three general aims will help you to adequately follow third-year courses, especially your BA Thesis.

contentFields.title: Aims
contentFields.text: 1. Learning objectives At the end of this course, the student will be able to reflect critically on primary literature in the area of intercultural communication, will have mastered the basic principles of setting up corpus research, will have learned to develop and test an analysis model and will have reported in the target language of a contrasting corpus analysis. Regarding the written examination, the student will demonstrate that they: Can explain and motivate the choice of literature Can reflect critically on the primary literature Can link the models used in the literature Can apply the analysis models used in the literature to new material With regard to the paper, in the form of a scientific article, the student demonstrates that they are able to: Accurately describe the method used Analyse and report the results In the conclusion/discussion section, place his/her results in the context of the research and scientific field and reflect on, as well as translate, the consequences of the research to the professional field Report scientifically in the target language on his/her research

contentFields.text: Attention: A basic knowledge of statistics and SPSS. To participate in Cross-Cultural Language Use Spanish, students must have obtained at least 10 of the 15 ECTS of Spanish-language courses from the B2 (i.e., 2 of the 3 subjects).

contentFields.title: Test information
contentFields.text: Examination: - Written examination based on information covered in the primary literature and lectures (after period 1) (40%) - Final paper about the collective contrastive corpus compiled for the target language. The introduction to this paper will be provided by the lecturers. Assessment will only take place on the basis of the following sections in the report: Research Question, Methodology, Results and Conclusion & Discussion. (60%) Participation in the lectures is not compulsory, but participation in the seminars is compulsory. If a student attends less than 65% of the seminars in period 2, they will be excluded from both the first and second opportunity to take the examination for this part of the course (= final paper). The student shall then be unable to complete the course in the relevant academic year. (EER): “A student who is absent from more than 35% of the lectures of a course in one period is excluded from further participation in the course and from the partial and interim examinations that are part of the course.” (see https://tinyurl.com/bdhhmkny ) Final papers must be uploaded via BRIGHTSPACE and, if requested by the lecturer, must also be submitted as hard copies. The hand-in time shown on BRIGHTSPACE will be used to determine whether the deadline was met. Students caught engaging in plagiarism will be reported to the Examining Board which will handle this issue (see https://www.ru.nl/facultyofarts/stip/rules-guidelines/education-assessment/fraud-plagiarism). If a student scores less than a 5.5 on the written examination or the research article, they must take the resit. If the course is not completed with a passing grade, the student must take the entire course again (partial grades will expire).

contentFields.title: Content
contentFields.text: The rise and spread of English as a global language and lingua franca in the world has allowed people with various cultural and linguistic backgrounds to communicate with one another in different contexts. The new linguistic landscape that has developed offers us opportunity to reflect on the linguistic, communicative, cultural, societal, psychological, economic and political issues that are related to the global use of English. This course is therefore multidisciplinary since it focuses on English as a global language from the perspectives of multiple research specializations, and includes both theoretical reflections and applied exercises. This allows students to develop the knowledge and skills necessary to understand the globalization of English in various settings and extrapolate their new competences to academic and real-world professional contexts.

contentFields.title: Aims
contentFields.text: At the end of the course students are able to: describe the main factors in the spread of English globally and how varieties of English have evolved. describe the various professional and informal communication contexts in which English is used, and how it has impacted culture, media, societies, various types of organizations, teams and individuals. analyze and reflect on effects of global English (use) from an individual language user's perspective on aspects such as identity formation, professional performance, well-being, linguistic exclusion, and discrimination. reflect on contrasting perspectives held by researchers on global English as a phenomenon. understand the general academic and societal relevance of knowledge on English as a global language. explain, summarize and discuss specialized course content to peers and general audiences in spoken and written contexts.

contentFields.title: Content
contentFields.text: Content Working on your personal and professional development (PPD) How to make the transition to university and from university to a professional career? Which skills would you like to develop further? During coaching sessions, individually or with a group of peers, you will ponder questions like these. We will challenge you to think about who you want to be as a person and an academic. Furthermore, you will set your own goals, devise strategies and act to achieve your goals. By consciously working on your PPD (personal and professional development) you will boost your self-confidence, self-reliance and resilience. This will help you grow into a conscientious, committed, critical and self-aware academic who is set up for lifelong learning and feels ready to play their part in society. In the course manual and on Brightspace you will find additional information about coaching sessions, groups, schedule and programme.

contentFields.title: Aims
contentFields.text: Aims At the end of the course, the student is able to reflect on their personal and professional development and shape this development by identifying and substantiating their own needs and insights and by making informed choices. by engaging in activities to the benefit of their own development in the program (and for the benefit of their future career)

contentFields.title: Test information
contentFields.text: Test information During your whole bachelor’s you will work on your personal and professional development (PPD) and you will record this development in a portfolio (Portflow). You will not be graded at the end of the Mentoring program, but instead the end result is a ‘pass’ or ‘no pass’. Successfully ending your mentoring program is your first milestone in the PPD learning trajectory. The time you spend on PPD and building up your portfolio, including the time you invest during this mentoring program, will be rewarded in a course in the last/third year of your bachelor’s.

contentFields.title: Content
contentFields.text: De afdeling Taal en Communicatie bereidt jou voor op je toekomst als wetenschapper en/of professional. Als aanvulling op de academische en vakinhoudelijke kennis die je tijdens je studie vergaarde, werd je uitgedaagd om na te denken over wie je wilt zijn als persoon en als academicus en/of professional. Je werkte enerzijds aan praktische vaardigheden die je nodig hebt op de arbeidsmarkt, anderzijds leerde je jezelf beter kennen, leerde je reflecteren op je sterktes, zwaktes, handelen en overtuigingen en leerde je jezelf doelen te stellen en acties te ondernemen om die doelen te bereiken. Door bewust te werken aan je Persoonlijke en Professionele Ontwikkeling (PPO) vergroot je je zelfvertrouwen, zelfstandigheid en veerkracht en krijg je een beter idee waar je naartoe werkt. Dit helpt je uit te groeien tot een gewetensvolle, betrokken, kritische en zelfbewuste academicus die een duurzame rol in de maatschappij kan innemen als professional en is voorbereid op een leven lang leren. PPO is binnen de Faculteit der Letteren gericht op drie thema’s: academische attitude, regie nemen en toekomst. In de eerste twee studiejaren (B1 en B2), werkte je vooral aan zelfregie, zelfstandigheid, reflectie en zelfvertrouwen. In het laatste studiejaar van de bachelor (de B3), staat afronding en profilering centraal: je verzamelt je opgedane PPO-ervaringen en reflecteert daarop in een afrondend PPO-portfolio, oriënteert je op je vervolgstappen (master of arbeidsmarkt) en ontwikkelt sollicitatie- en netwerkvaardigheden die je helpen jouw kwaliteiten zichtbaar te maken voor de buitenwereld. Daarnaast ga je in deze cursus aan de slag met je verworven professionele en persoonlijke vaardigheden in een denktank. De denktank is het onderdeel van de PPO cursus waarin je in een team onder begeleiding van een docent een maatschappelijk vraagstuk onderzoekt op het terrein van taal en communicatie. Je werkt toe naar een eindproduct dat de maatschappelijk partner zal helpen om het vraagstuk op adequate wijze aan te pakken. Tijdens het proces zul je nieuwe kennis en vaardigheden opdoen door van elkaar te leren terwijl je samen aan het project werkt. Jullie zijn als team zelf verantwoordelijk voor het groepsproces en de communicatie met de maatschappelijke partner. Je doorloopt in de denktank een traject van het formuleren van een doelstelling, via het bepalen van de aanpak, het verdelen van taken en het opzetten en uitvoeren van het project tot en met de presentatie van het eindproduct. De docent begeleidt jullie bij dit proces en beoordeelt het al dan niet behalen van de cursus aan de hand van verschillende (tussentijdse) producten.

contentFields.title: Aims
contentFields.text: Na afloop van deze B3 PPO cursus kun je als student: 1) een persoonlijk portfolio waarin je je ontwikkeling zichtbaar maakt, opbouwen en onderhouden. 2) je eigen verhaal vormgeven: je eigen profiel ontwikkelen, verbanden leggen tussen je studie en je toekomstmogelijkheden en een eindreflectie schrijven op je leerproces, vaardigheden en loopbaanoriëntatie. 3) inzichten en oplossingen bieden voor een maatschappelijk vraagstuk door jouw kennis en vaardigheden in te zetten in een (onderzoeks)project; 4) in teamverband een projectplan opstellen voor een (onderzoeks)project, waarin je het project definieert en afbakent en de projectactiviteiten beschrijft en plant; 5) in teamverband de projectactiviteiten verdelen en uitvoeren en hierbij constructief samenwerken, rekening houdend met de verschillende belangen van de betrokken partijen; 6) de resultaten van het (onderzoeks)project op een heldere en voor de betrokken partijen relevante manier presenteren; 7) reflecteren op je eigen kwaliteiten en op de ontwikkeling die je hebt doorgemaakt bij het werken in een team en het uitvoeren van het project.

contentFields.title: Content
contentFields.text: Although the role of English as a lingua franca in business contexts is undisputed, IBC research has shown that the use of English can cause problems for professionals who do not speak English as their mother tongue. When non-native speakers communicate in English, their English will differ from native speakers. The question is to what extent this different language use may cause communication problems. In this course, you will study the theory and methodology of research in the field of non-nativeness in international business communication on the basis of English articles. You will analyse the articles and ask critical questions about them. You will carry out SPSS assignments in which you analyse sample data. You will report on a small-scale experimental study into the effect of an aspect of non-nativeness. During the course you will (individually) work on analysing data and writing the different sections of an English research paper about the experimental study, resulting in a full-fledged English research paper at the end of the course.

contentFields.title: Aims
contentFields.text: At the end of the course, students: - are able to critically assess academic literature in the field of non-nativeness in English in international business communication - can apply their knowledge of non-nativeness in analysing and reporting an experimental study into the effect of an aspect of non-nativeness in English on the recipient of a message - can analyse the results of this study and report in English at C1 level.

contentFields.title: Content
contentFields.text: English is the lingua franca in international organizations, the business community, and in the academic world. This course aims to optimize the level of English of IBC students at the end of the Bachelor programme, and to prepare them for a certified English test (such as CAE and CPE), which, increasingly, is a job requirement. These recognized tests certify the language level of a candidate with regard to the four skills: reading, listening, writing and speaking skills. In this course, the student practises these skills in a variety of individual assignments (including 'business cases') to optimize his/her/their level of English (CEFR range: advanced user). The focus in this course is on both academic and business English, and on productive skills (speaking and writing), as these are the skills that students will need most in their future positions.

contentFields.title: Aims
contentFields.text: At the end of the course, students can: - communicate in English when writing about subjects relevant to international business communication (e.g. crisis communication, 'startups', social media policy) - in a series of individual writing assignments in academic and professional contexts (e.g. management reports, social media case analysis, crisis communication advice, editorial, press release) - at CEFR level C1/C2.

conditions.title: Presumed foreknowledge
conditions.text: Bachelor students IBC are only allowed to start with the thesis at the beginning of the second semester of the third bachelor year.

contentFields.title: Content
contentFields.text: In this course, you will conduct research on an aspect of international business communication. Examples of research topics include the effect of non-native accentedness on listeners, the use of foreign languages in marketing as a tool to attract customers, cultural standardisation or adaptation of communication or language choice in corporate narratives. Whichever topic you choose, the research question must be inspired by a debate in recent scientific literature, the study must be designed and implemented in a methodical way, and the results must be presented in an article intended for publication in a scientific journal. Depending on the question, the research may be quantitative (corpus analysis/experiment) or qualitative (interviews/observations) in nature. You will complete all steps in the research process together with your fellow students (from reading relevant literature to reporting on your results in a scientifically sound manner). There are two intake moments for the bachelor's thesis: at the start of period 1 and at the start of period 3. You need to register for a theme before the start of the semester in which you want to do the Bachelor's thesis (in August or January). You must register for the course via Osiris and for a theme via the theme choice form (online via Brightspace).

contentFields.title: Aims
contentFields.text: At the end of the course, students will be capable of: • Finding, understanding and using relevant literature with the aim of formulating and substantiating a research question; • Setting up a useful, feasible, valid and reliable research study to answer the research question; • Answering a research question by analysing and interpreting the data obtained; • Linking the research results to the existing literature and the professional field; • Reporting on these results in the form of an academic paper.
